summary: Describes the Camellia encryption algorithm, a block cipher with a 128-bit block size and keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits. The document gives the algorithm, including its key schedule and data-mixing steps. It is informational, meant to let implementers work from a public description.

plainLanguage.summary: Camellia is a recipe for scrambling a message into gibberish using a secret key, so only someone with the same key can unscramble it.

questions: how many rounds does camellia have
subtitle: A public description of Camellia, a 128-bit block cipher with the same interface as AES.

tldr.problem: Implementers needed a written description of the Camellia block cipher, which was developed by NTT and Mitsubishi Electric, so they could build interoperable versions.
tldr.mechanism: Camellia encrypts a 128-bit block with a Feistel structure of 18 rounds (128-bit keys) or 24 rounds (192- and 256-bit keys), with FL and FLINV functions inserted every 6 rounds and subkeys produced by a key schedule.
tldr.outcome: The RFC also defines object identifiers for CBC mode and gives test data. It is Informational, not a standard, and states that Camellia was recommended by NESSIE and listed by CRYPTREC.

today: RFC 3713 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the written description of the Camellia algorithm, and it does not itself specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: What Camellia Is
sections.content:
Camellia is a block cipher jointly developed by Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation and Mitsubishi Electric Corporation in 2000. It uses a 128-bit block size and 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys, the same interface as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).

The authors describe it as suitable for both software and hardware, including 32-bit processors, 8-bit processors in smart cards, cryptographic hardware and embedded systems. They also claim excellent key setup time and key agility superior to AES. The RFC says Camellia was selected as a recommended primitive by the EU NESSIE project and included in the list of techniques for Japanese e-Government systems selected by CRYPTREC.
sections.plainLanguage: Camellia is a lock-and-key system for messages. It works on one 16-byte chunk at a time and comes with three sizes of key, bigger being harder to guess.

sections.title: The Key Schedule
sections.content:
The algorithm has a key scheduling part and a data randomizing part. The key schedule first splits the secret key K into two 128-bit values, KL and KR. For a 128-bit key, KL is K and KR is 0. For a 192-bit key, KL is the leftmost 128 bits and KR is the rightmost 64 bits followed by the complement of those 64 bits. For a 256-bit key, KL is the left half and KR the right half.

From KL and KR the schedule derives two more 128-bit values, KA and KB, using the F-function and six 64-bit constants called Sigma1 to Sigma6. Then 64-bit subkeys are produced by rotating KL, KR, KA and KB and taking the left or right half. A 128-bit key gives kw1 to kw4, k1 to k18 and ke1 to ke4. A 192- or 256-bit key gives kw1 to kw4, k1 to k24 and ke1 to ke6. KB is used only for 192- and 256-bit keys.
sections.plainLanguage: First the secret key is stirred and chopped into many smaller keys. Each step of scrambling later uses its own small key.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting a Block
sections.content:
The 128-bit plaintext is split into a left 64-bit half D1 and a right 64-bit half D2. Encryption is a Feistel structure: 18 rounds for 128-bit keys and 24 rounds for 192- and 256-bit keys. Each round XORs one half with the output of the F-function applied to the other half and a subkey. Before the rounds, D1 and D2 are XORed with kw1 and kw2 (prewhitening). After the rounds, the halves are XORed with kw3 and kw4 (postwhitening). The ciphertext is D2 followed by D1.

Every 6 rounds, the FL-function is applied to D1 and the FLINV-function to D2, each with a ke subkey. Decryption uses the same procedure with the subkeys in reverse order, for example k1 swapped with k18 for a 128-bit key and with k24 for the longer keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The block is cut into two halves. The halves take turns scrambling each other, round after round. To undo it, you do the same dance with the small keys in the opposite order.

sections.title: The F, FL and FLINV Functions
sections.content:
The F-function takes a 64-bit input and a 64-bit subkey. It XORs them, splits the result into eight bytes, replaces each byte through one of four lookup tables (SBOX1 to SBOX4), and then mixes the eight bytes with a fixed pattern of XORs to produce 64 bits. SBOX1 is given as a table in the RFC; SBOX2, SBOX3 and SBOX4 are defined from it by rotations.

The FL-function works on two 32-bit halves of a 64-bit input and a 64-bit subkey, using AND, OR, XOR and a one-bit left rotation. FLINV is its inverse function.
sections.plainLanguage: The F-function is the blender in the middle: it swaps every byte using a lookup table, then mixes them all together so one small change spreads everywhere.

sections.title: Object Identifiers for CBC Mode
sections.content:
The RFC defines three object identifiers, one for each key size, for Camellia in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode: id-camellia128-cbc, id-camellia192-cbc and id-camellia256-cbc. They sit under the arc iso(1) member-body(2) 392 200011 61 and end in 2, 3 and 4 respectively.

These algorithms need an initialization vector, carried as CamelliaIV, an OCTET STRING of size 16. When these identifiers are used, plaintext is padded before encryption as in RFC 2315.
sections.plainLanguage: Each version of Camellia gets a unique name tag so computers can say exactly which one they are using. Chaining mode also needs a random starting value, 16 bytes long.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The authors say they evaluated Camellia with state-of-the-art cryptanalytic techniques. They confirmed it has no differential or linear characteristics that hold with probability more than 2^(-128), which they say makes differential and linear attacks extremely unlikely to succeed against the full 18-round version. They also state it was designed to resist higher order differential, interpolation, related-key and truncated differential attacks, among others.

These are the authors' own claims, backed by references to their papers. Appendix A of the RFC provides test data in hexadecimal for 128-, 192- and 256-bit keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The inventors tried many known ways to crack their own lock and report that none looks likely to work. They also give example inputs and outputs so you can check your own copy.
